text: Bernard Sanders, born on September 8, 1941, in Brooklyn, New York, is an American politician and activist serving as the senior United States senator from Vermont, a seat he has held since 2007. He is the longest-serving independent in U.S. congressional history but maintains a close relationship with the Democratic Party, having caucused with House and Senate Democrats for most of his congressional career and sought the party's presidential nomination in 2016 and 2020. Ideologically a democratic socialist, Sanders is regarded as one of the main leaders of the modern American progressive movement. Born into a working-class Jewish family, Sanders attended Brooklyn College from 1959 to 1960 before transferring to the University of Chicago, where he graduated with a Bachelor of Arts in political science in 1964. While a student, he was a protest organizer for the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) and the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC) during the civil rights movement. In 1962, he protested the University of Chicago's segregated housing policy by entering the administration building and camping outside the president's office, leading to the end of racial segregation in private university housing by 1963. He also attended the 1963 March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, where Martin Luther King Jr. delivered the "I Have a Dream" speech, and was fined $25 (equivalent to $257 in 2024) for resisting arrest during a demonstration against segregation in Chicago's public schools. Sanders opposed the Vietnam War and applied for conscientious objector status, though his application was denied due to age. He later worked with the United Packinghouse Workers of America and supported Leon Despres's reelection campaign. After graduating, he worked as a Head Start teacher, psychiatric aide, and carpenter in New York City before moving to Stannard, Vermont, in 1968, where he lived for several years and worked as a carpenter, filmmaker, and writer, creating educational materials and articles for The Vermont Freeman. In 1972, he ran as a Liberty Union candidate for governor and in a special election for U.S. senator, finishing third in the 1974 senatorial race with 5,901 votes (4%). He later ran for mayor of Burlington in 1980, winning by 22 votes initially, later reduced to 10, defeating incumbent Gordon Paquette, Richard Bove, and Joseph McGrath. He was reelected in 1982 and 1984, and announced a fourth term in 1986, defeating Democratic nominee Paul Lafayette. He stated he would not seek another mayoral term after 1987. During his mayoralty, Sanders called himself a socialist and led efforts to balance the city's budget, attract a minor league baseball team, fund community-trust housing, and successfully sue the local cable television franchise for reduced rates. He also revitalized the Lake Champlain waterfront, opposing plans to convert it into luxury condominiums and hotels, instead supporting a mixed-use district with housing, parks, and public spaces. He hosted a public-access television program, Bernie Speaks with the Community, from 1986 to 1988, and collaborated with 30 Vermont musicians to record a folk album, We Shall Overcome, in 1987. In 1985, he hosted a foreign policy speech by Noam Chomsky. In 1988, he traveled to the Soviet Union to interview the mayor of Yaroslavl about housing and health care. Sanders was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1990, representing Vermont's at-large congressional district. In 1991, he co-founded the Congressional Progressive Caucus with five other House members. He served in the House for 16 years before being elected to the U.S. Senate in 2006, becoming the first non-Republican elected to Vermont's Class 1 seat since Solomon Foot, a Whig, in 1850. He was reelected in 2012, 2018, and 2024. He chaired the Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee from 2013 to 2015, the Senate Budget Committee from 2021 to 2023, and the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee from 2023 to 2025. He is the senior senator and dean of the Vermont congressional delegation. Sanders ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2016 and 2020, finishing second both times. His 2016 campaign generated significant grassroots enthusiasm and funding from small-dollar donors, helping him win 23 primaries and caucuses. In 2020, he was a front-runner in the Democratic field. After the 2020 primaries, he became a close ally of Joe Biden. Since Donald Trump's reelection as president in 2024, Sanders has vocally opposed Trump's administration and perceived corruption, calling it a right-wing oligarchy, and has rallied an organization tour against Trump and his allies, especially Elon Musk, to reshape the Democratic Party. Sanders is credited with influencing a leftward shift in the Democratic Party after his 2016 campaign. He opposes neoliberalism and supports workers' self-management, universal and single-payer healthcare, paid parental leave, tuition-free tertiary education, a Green New Deal, and worker control of production through cooperatives, unions, and democratic public enterprises. On foreign policy, he supports reducing military spending, more diplomacy and international cooperation, and greater emphasis on labor rights and environmental concerns in international trade agreements. He supports workplace democracy and has praised elements of the Nordic model. His father, Elias Ben Yehuda Sanders, a Polish-Jewish immigrant born in Słopnice, Austrian Galicia (now in Poland), immigrated to the United States in 1921 and became a paint salesman. His mother, Dorothy Sanders (née Glassberg), was born in New York City. He is the younger brother of Larry Sanders. Sanders became interested in politics early due to his family background, including the Holocaust-related deaths of many relatives in German-occupied Poland in the 1940s. He lived in Midwood, Brooklyn, attended P.S. 197, won a borough championship on the basketball team, and attended Hebrew school, celebrating his bar mitzvah in 1954. His older brother Larry noted that the family never lacked food or clothing, but major purchases like curtains or a rug were not affordable. In high school, he was captain of the track team and took third place in the New York City indoor one-mile race. He lost his first election for student body president but became active in fundraising for Korean War orphans. He attended high school with economist Walter Block. When he was 19, his mother died at age 47, and his father died two years later in 1962 at age 57. Sanders described his college experience as "boring and irrelevant" and emphasized community activism as more important to his education. He described his time in Chicago as "the major period of intellectual ferment in my life." He joined the Young People's Socialist League and was active in civil rights protests, including sit-ins that led to the end of racial segregation in private university housing. In 1971, while researching for Liberty Union's newspaper Movement, he stayed at Myrtle Hill Farm, a back-to-the-land commune, but was asked to leave after three days for failing to contribute physical labor. Some residents complained that he distracted them from work. In 1980, he was one of three electors for the Socialist Workers Party in Vermont. After resigning from the Liberty Union Party in 1977, he worked as a writer and director of the American People's Historical Society, producing a documentary on Eugene V. Debs. On October 25, 2025, the Eugene V. Debs Foundation awarded him its namesake award. In 1988, he traveled to the Soviet Union to interview the mayor of Yaroslavl about housing and health care.

In the 1980s, U.S. foreign policy in Latin America was a significant focus. In 1985, Burlington City Hall hosted a foreign policy speech by Noam Chomsky, who was introduced as "a very vocal and important voice in the wilderness of intellectual life in America" and described as someone "we're all very proud of." From 1986 to 1988, Bernie Sanders hosted and produced a public-access television program called Bernie Speaks with the Community. In 1987, he collaborated with 30 Vermont musicians to record a folk album titled We Shall Overcome. That same year, US News & World Report ranked Sanders one of America's best mayors. As of 2013, Burlington was regarded as one of the most livable cities in the United States. During a 1988 trip to the Soviet Union, Sanders interviewed the mayor of Burlington's sister city, Yaroslavl, on housing and health care issues. When Sanders left office in 1989, city council member Bouricius stated that he had "changed the entire nature of politics in Burlington and also in the state of Vermont." In 1988, incumbent Republican congressman Jim Jeffords ran for the U.S. Senate, vacating the House seat for Vermont's at-large district. Former lieutenant governor Peter P. Smith won the House election with 41% of the vote, Sanders, running as an independent, placed second with 38%, and Democratic state representative Paul N. Poirier placed third with 19%. Two years later, Sanders ran again and defeated Smith by a margin of 56% to 39%. Sanders was the first independent elected to the U.S. House of Representatives since Frazier Reams of Ohio won his second term in 1952 and the first socialist elected to the House since Vito Marcantonio of the American Labor Party won his last term in 1948. Sanders served in the House from 1991 until he became a senator in 2007, winning reelection by large margins except during the 1994 Republican Revolution, when he won by 3% with 50% of the vote. During his first year in the House, Sanders often alienated allies and colleagues by criticizing both political parties for serving the wealthy. In 1991, he co-founded the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which he chaired for its first eight years, while refusing to join the Democratic Party or caucus. In 2005, Rolling Stone called Sanders the "amendment king" for passing more roll call amendments than any other congressman since 1995, when Congress was under Republican control, due to his ability to form coalitions across party lines. In 1999, Sanders voted against rolling back Glass–Steagall legislation that separated investment and commercial banks. He was a vocal critic of Federal Reserve Chair Alan Greenspan, stating in June 2003 that he was "way out of touch" and saw his role as representing the wealthy and large corporations. On February 7, 1992, Sanders sponsored the Cancer Registries Amendment Act to establish cancer registries to collect data on cancer; Senator Patrick Leahy introduced a companion bill in the Senate on October 2, 1992, which was passed by the House on October 6 and signed into law by President George H. W. Bush on October 24, 1992. In 1993, Sanders voted against the Brady Bill, which mandated federal background checks and waiting periods for gun purchases, a bill that passed 238–187; he opposed it four more times in the 1990s, arguing that Vermont constituents viewed waiting-period mandates as a state matter. Sanders did vote for other gun-control measures, such as the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act in 1994, which included the Violence Against Women Act and a ban on certain assault weapons, though he criticized other parts of the bill. He acknowledged that some people are deeply violent and must be incarcerated but argued that repressive policies doom millions of young people to violence and that society should focus on creating jobs instead of building more jails. In 1996, he voted against a bill that would have prohibited police from purchasing tanks and armored carriers. In 1998, he voted for a bill increasing minimum sentencing for possessing a gun while committing a federal crime to ten years, including nonviolent marijuana possession. In 2005, Sanders voted for the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, which prevented firearms manufacturers and dealers from being held liable for negligence in crimes involving their products; as of 2016, he said he had changed his position and would vote to defeat the bill. Sanders was a consistent critic of the Patriot Act, voting against the original legislation and sponsoring and voting for amendments to curtail its effects, while voting against each reauthorization. In June 2005, he proposed an amendment to limit the government's access to individuals' library and book-buying records, which passed the House by a bipartisan majority but was removed in House–Senate negotiations and never became law. Sanders voted against the resolutions authorizing the use of force against Iraq in 1991 and 2002 and opposed the 2003 invasion of Iraq. He voted for the 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Terrorists, cited as the legal justification for military actions after September 11. He opposed the Bush administration's unilateral decision to start a war. In February 2005, Sanders introduced a bill to withdraw the permanent normal trade relations status extended to China in 2000, stating that U.S. trade policy with China was a failure and had led to job losses, though the bill received 71 co-sponsors and was not sent to a vote. Sanders entered the U.S. Senate race on April 21, 2005, after Senator Jim Jeffords announced he would not seek a fourth term. Chuck Schumer, a fellow James Madison High School alumnus and chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, endorsed Sanders. This meant no Democrat could expect financial support from the party. He was also endorsed by Senate minority leader Harry Reid and Democratic National Committee chair Howard Dean, who said in May 2005 that Sanders "votes with the Democrats 98% of the time." Then-Senator Barack Obama campaigned for him in Vermont in March 2006. Sanders entered into an agreement with the Democratic Party to be listed in their primary but to decline the nomination if he won, which he did. The 2006 campaign was the most expensive in Vermont's history, and Sanders defeated businessman Rich Tarrant by an almost 2-to-1 margin, with many national media outlets projecting a win shortly after polls closed. Sanders was reelected in 2012 with 71% of the vote, defeating Republican nominee John MacGovern. He was reelected in 2018 with 67% of the vote, defeating Republican nominee Lawrence Zupan. On May 6, 2024, Sanders announced his candidacy for a fourth Senate term; a poll just weeks earlier found over half of respondents wanted him to seek reelection. He faced Republican nominee Gerald Malloy, who had run against Senator Peter Welch in 2022. Sanders was reelected and stated this term would likely be his last. While in Congress, Sanders sponsored 15 concurrent resolutions and 15 Senate resolutions; of those co-sponsored, 218 became law. Politico noted he has "rarely forged actual legislation or left a significant imprint on it," and The New York Times stated that "big legislation largely eludes Mr. Sanders because his ideas are usually far to the left of the majority of the Senate... Mr. Sanders has largely found ways to press his agenda through appending small provisions to the larger bills of others." During his Senate tenure, he had lower legislative effectiveness than the average senator, as measured by the number of sponsored bills that passed and successful amendments made. Nevertheless, he sponsored over 500 amendments to bills, many of which became law. These amendments resulted in a ban on imported goods made by child labor; $100 million in funding for community health centers; $10 million for a mental health outreach program for service members with PTSD, traumatic brain injury, depression, panic attacks, and other disorders; a public database of senior Department of Defense officials seeking employment with defense contractors; and inclusion of autism treatment under the military healthcare program Tricare. In August 2022, Sanders voted for the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, though he called it only a small step forward. He joined Democrats to pass the bill, which capped insulin costs for Medicare seniors at $35 a month and allowed Medicare to negotiate lower drug prices. In 2008 and 2009, Sanders voted against the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), a program to purchase toxic banking assets and provide loans to failing banks. On February 4, 2009, he sponsored an amendment to ensure TARP funds would not displace U.S. workers, which passed and was included in the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009. Among his proposed financial reforms is auditing the Federal Reserve, which would reduce its independence in monetary policy; Federal Reserve officials say such legislation would expose the Fed to undue political pressure. On December 10, 2010, Sanders delivered an 8-hour and 34-minute speech against the Tax Relief, Unemployment Insurance Reauthorization, and Job Creation Act of 2010, which extended Bush-era tax rates. He argued the legislation favored the wealthy and asked, "How many homes can you own?" The bill passed the Senate with a strong majority and was signed into law a week later. In February 2011, Nation Books published the speech as The Speech: A Historic Filibuster on Corporate Greed and the Decline of Our Middle Class, with proceeds going to Vermont nonprofit organizations. In 2016, Sanders voted for the Federal Reserve Transparency Act, which included proposals for a reformed audit of the Federal Reserve System. On June 12, 2017, U.S. senators agreed to legislation imposing new sanctions on Russia and Iran; the bill was opposed only by Sanders and Republican Rand Paul. He supported sanctions on Russia but voted against the bill because he believed the sanctions could endanger the Iran nuclear deal. In 2018, Sanders sponsored a bill with senators Chris Murphy (D–CT) and Mike Lee (R–UT) to invoke the 1973 War Powers Resolution to end U.S. support for the Saudi-led military intervention in Yemen, which has caused hundreds of thousands of civilian deaths and millions more to suffer from starvation and disease. After the October 2018 assassination of Jamal Khashoggi, which was ordered by Saudi crown prince Mohammad bin Salman, the bill attracted bipartisan co-sponsors and passed the Senate 56–41. It passed the House 247–175 in February 2019 and was vetoed by President Trump, who said it was "an unnecessary, dangerous attempt to weaken my constitutional authorities, endangering the lives of American citizens and brave service members, both today and in the future." During the Gaza war, Sanders introduced several Joint Resolutions of Disapproval to block arms to Israel; all failed, but in November 2024, one garnered support from 18 senators, in April 2025 from 15, and in July 2025 from 27 senators, a majority of Senate Democrats. In mid-December 2009, Sanders successfully added a provision to the Affordable Care Act to fund $11 billion for community health centers, especially in rural areas, helping secure the 60 votes needed for passage. On May 4, 2017, in response to the House vote to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act, Sanders predicted "thousands of Americans would die" from losing access to health care, a statement rated "mostly true" by PolitiFact. In September 2017, Sanders and 15 Senate co-sponsors introduced the Medicare for All bill, a single-payer healthcare plan that includes vision and dental care, unlike Medicare. Some Republicans called it "Berniecare" or "the latest Democratic push for socialized medicine and higher taxes." Sanders responded that the Republican Party has no credibility on healthcare after voting to remove health insurance from 32 million Americans under the Affordable Care Act. As chairman of the Senate Subcommittee on Primary Health and Aging, Sanders introduced legislation in 2013 to reauthorize and strengthen the Older Americans Act, supporting programs like Meals on Wheels for seniors. In 2007, Sanders helped kill a comprehensive immigration reform bill, arguing its guest-worker program would depress wages for American workers. In 2010, he supported the DREAM Act, which would have provided a path to citizenship for undocumented minors. In 2013, he supported the Gang of Eight's comprehensive immigration reform bill after securing a $1.5 billion youth jobs program provision, which he said would offset labor market competition with immigrants. In a March 2025 interview, Sanders said Biden failed to curb illegal immigration and commended Trump for strengthening border policies, stating "nobody thinks illegal immigration is appropriate," while criticizing mass deportations and calling for comprehensive reform. In April 2017, Sanders introduced a bill to raise the minimum wage for federal contract workers to $15 an hour, an increase over a prior $12 proposal. On May 9, 2018, he introduced the Workplace Democracy Act, which would expand labor rights by making it easier for workers to join unions, banning right-to-work laws and some anti-union provisions of the Taft–Hartley Act, and outlawing certain union-busting tactics. Announcing the legislation, he said, "If we are serious about reducing income and wealth inequality and rebuilding the middle class, we have got to substantially increase the number of union jobs in this country." Sanders opposed the 2018 federal budget proposed by the Trump administration, calling it "a budget for the billionaire class, for Wall Street, for corporate CEOs, and for the wealthiest people in this country... nothing less than a massive transfer."

Sanders criticized Biden for failing to adequately curb illegal immigration and praised Trump for strengthening border immigration policies, stating that "nobody thinks illegal immigration is appropriate," while also condemning mass deportations and advocating for comprehensive immigration reform. In April 2017, he introduced a bill to raise the minimum wage for federal contract workers to $15 an hour, surpassing an earlier Democratic proposal of $12 an hour. On May 9, 2018, he introduced the Workplace Democracy Act, which would expand labor rights by making it easier for workers to join unions, ban right-to-work laws and certain anti-union provisions of the Taft–Hartley Act, and outlaw specific union-busting tactics. Announcing the bill, he stated, "If we are serious about reducing income and wealth inequality and rebuilding the middle class, we have got to substantially increase the number of union jobs in this country." Sanders opposed the 2018 federal budget proposed by the Trump administration, calling it "a budget for the billionaire class, for Wall Street, for corporate CEOs, and for the wealthiest people in this country... nothing less than a massive transfer of wealth from working families, the elderly, children, the sick and the poor to the top 1%." After the November 2017 Paradise Papers revelations and a report from the Institute for Policy Studies indicating that just three individuals—Jeff Bezos, Bill Gates, and Warren Buffett—own more wealth than the bottom half of the U.S. population, Sanders declared that "we must end global oligarchy" and asserted that "we need, in the United States and throughout the world, a tax system which is fair, progressive and transparent." On September 5, 2018, Sanders partnered with Ro Khanna to introduce the Stop Bad Employers by Zeroing Out Subsidies (Stop BEZOS) Act, which would require large corporations to pay for the food stamps and Medicaid benefits their employees receive, thereby reducing taxpayer burden. On June 9, 2014, Sanders sponsored the Veterans' Access to Care through Choice, Accountability, and Transparency Act of 2014 to reform the Department of Veterans Affairs following the 2014 Veterans Health Administration scandal, working with Senator John McCain, who co-sponsored the bill. His legislation was incorporated into the House version, passed by both chambers on July 31, 2014, and signed into law by President Obama on August 7, 2014. On March 17, 2016, Sanders expressed support for Merrick Garland's Supreme Court nomination, though he added that "there are some more progressive judges out there," and opposed Neil Gorsuch's nomination, stating that Gorsuch had "refused to answer legitimate questions." He also criticized Senate Republicans' use of the nuclear option to "choke off debate and ram [Gorsuch's] nomination through the Senate," and voted against Gorsuch's confirmation as an associate justice, as well as against Trump's nominees Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. In 2022, he voted to confirm Joe Biden's nominee Ketanji Brown Jackson to the Supreme Court. As an independent, Sanders maintains an agreement with Senate Democratic leadership where he votes with Democrats on procedural matters unless the Democratic whip, Dick Durbin, agrees he need not—such requests are rarely made or granted. In return, he retained his seniority and received committee seats that would have been available to him as a Democrat; in 2013–14, he chaired the United States Senate Committee on Veterans' Affairs during the Veterans Health Administration scandal. Sanders became the ranking minority member on the Senate Budget Committee in 2015 and its chair in 2021; he previously chaired the Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee for two years and has been chair of the Senate Democratic Outreach Committee since 2017. He appointed economics professor Stephanie Kelton, a modern monetary theory scholar, as chief economic adviser for the committee's Democratic minority and presented a report on rebuilding the disappearing middle class that included proposals to raise the minimum wage, boost infrastructure spending, and increase Social Security payments. Sanders was only the third senator from Vermont to caucus with the Democrats, after Jeffords and Leahy. His caucusing with the Democrats gave them a 51–49 majority in the Senate during the 110th Congress in 2007–08, as the Democrats needed 51 seats to control the Senate due to Vice President Dick Cheney likely breaking potential ties in favor of the Republicans. He is a member of various caucuses. A Public Policy Polling survey in August 2011 found Sanders had a 67% approval rating and a 28% disapproval rating, making him the third-most popular U.S. senator at the time. Both the NAACP and the NHLA gave him 100% voting scores during his tenure. In 2015, he was named one of the Top 5 of The Forward 50. A November 2015 Morning Consult poll found he had an 83% approval rating among constituents, making him the most popular U.S. senator. Fox News found him to have the highest net favorability at +28 points among prominent politicians in its March 2017 poll. He ranked third in 2014 and first in both 2015 and 2016. In April 2017, a nationwide Harvard-Harris Poll found Sanders had the highest favorability rating among all political figures in the poll, a standing confirmed by subsequent polling. During the 2012 Democratic presidential primaries, Sanders, dissatisfied with President Obama's "attempts to trade Social Security cuts for tax hikes," reportedly considered running against him and had previously suggested in 2011 that it was "a good idea" for someone to challenge Obama, getting so close to running that Senator Harry Reid had to intervene. In November 2013, Sanders suggested that Senator Elizabeth Warren could be president and that she might earn his backing if she ran, adding that if no progressive candidate ran, he might feel compelled to do so himself. In December 2014, Warren said she was not running. On April 30, 2015, Sanders announced his intention to seek the Democratic Party's presidential nomination. His campaign was officially launched on May 26 in Burlington. In his announcement, he stated, "I don't believe that the men and women who defended American democracy fought to create a situation where billionaires own the political process" and made this a central theme of his campaign. Warren welcomed Sanders's entry, saying, "I'm glad to see him get out there and give his version of what leadership in this country should be," but never endorsed him. Initially considered a long shot, Sanders won 23 primaries and caucuses and approximately 46% of pledged delegates to Hillary Clinton's 54%. His campaign was noted for its supporters' enthusiasm and for rejecting large donations from corporations, the financial industry, and associated Super PACs. Leaked Democratic National Committee (DNC) emails from June and July 2016 showed that committee leadership favored Clinton over Sanders and worked to help her win the nomination. On July 12, 2016, Sanders formally endorsed Clinton in her unsuccessful general election campaign against Donald Trump, urging his supporters to continue the "political revolution" his campaign had begun. Following the endorsement, Sanders campaigned for Clinton for weeks, holding 39 rallies in 13 states during the final three months before the 2016 election. Unlike other major candidates, Sanders did not pursue funding through a Super PAC or from wealthy donors, instead focusing on small-dollar donations. His campaign raised $1.5 million within 24 hours of the official announcement and, by year's end, had raised a total of $73 million from over one million people, making 2.5 million donations with an average donation of $27.16. By the end of January 2016, the campaign had reached 3.25 million donations, raising $20 million in that month alone. Sanders used social media to gain momentum, posting content on Twitter and Facebook and answering questions on Reddit, building a large grassroots online following. A July 29, 2015, online meetup brought 100,000 supporters to more than 3,500 simultaneous events nationwide. To his surprise, Sanders's June 2015 campaign events drew overflow crowds across the country. When Clinton and Sanders made public appearances within days of each other in Des Moines, Iowa, Sanders drew larger crowds, even though he had already made many stops in the state and Clinton's visit was her first in 2015. On July 1, 2015, his campaign stop in Madison, Wisconsin, drew the largest crowd of any 2016 presidential candidate to that date, with an estimated turnout of 10,000. Over the following weeks, he drew even larger crowds: 11,000 in Phoenix; 15,000 in Seattle; and 28,000 in Portland, Oregon. Critics alleged that the small number of debates and the schedule—half on Saturday or Sunday nights—were part of the DNC's deliberate effort to protect Clinton, who was perceived as the front-runner. In February 2016, both campaigns agreed in principle to hold four more debates for a total of ten. Clinton dropped out of the tenth debate, scheduled just before the California primary, citing a need to focus on direct contact with California voters and general election preparation. Sanders expressed disappointment that Clinton canceled the debate before what he believed would be "the largest and most important primary in the presidential nominating process." Some Sanders supporters raised concerns that publications like The New York Times minimized coverage of his campaign in favor of others, especially Trump and Clinton. The Times' ombudsman found that as of September 2015, the paper "hasn't always taken it very seriously" and that some stories were dismissive or mocking, focusing on his age, appearance, and style rather than his policies. Coverage of Sanders was significantly less than that of Trump, despite similar polling results—63 articles on Trump versus 14 on Sanders. A December 2015 report found that the three major networks—CBS, NBC, and ABC—spent 234 minutes on Trump and only 10 minutes on Sanders, with ABC World News Tonight spending 81 minutes on Trump and less than one minute on Sanders during 2015. A study of media coverage in the 2016 election concluded that while Sanders received less coverage than Hillary Clinton, the amount of coverage was largely consistent with his polling performance, except in 2015 when coverage exceeded his polling standing. Studies found that the tone of media coverage of Sanders was more favorable than any other candidate, while Clinton received the most negative coverage. All 2016 candidates received vastly less media coverage than Donald Trump, and the Democratic primary received substantially less coverage than the Republican primary. Amy Goodman of Democracy Now! noted that on March 15, Super Tuesday III, the speeches of Trump, Clinton, Marco Rubio, and Ted Cruz were broadcast in full, while Sanders was speaking at a rally larger than any of the others in Phoenix, Arizona, yet his speech was not mentioned or broadcast. Political scientist Rachel Bitecofer wrote in her 2018 book that the Democratic primary was effectively over by mid-March 2016, but the media promoted the narrative that the Sanders–Clinton contest was "heating up" at that time. An NBC/Wall Street Journal poll in May 2016 found Clinton and Trump in a "dead heat," but if Sanders were the Democratic nominee, 53% of voters would support him to 39% for Trump. Clinton and Trump were the least popular likely candidates ever polled, with Sanders receiving a 43% positive and 36% negative rating. Polls showed that Democratic voters over 50 preferred Clinton by a large margin, while those under 50 overwhelmingly favored Sanders. A 2017 Newsweek analysis found that 12% of those who voted for Sanders in the Democratic primary voted for Trump in the general election, a lower proportion than that of Clinton supporters in 2008 who voted for John McCain. In July 2016, leaked DNC emails appeared to show officials favoring Clinton over Sanders, with staff discussing making his irreligious tendencies a potential issue in southern states and questioning his party loyalty. DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz called his campaign manager "an ass" and "a damn liar." Speaking with Jake Tapper on CNN, Sanders responded, saying, "it is an outrage and sad that you would have people in important positions in the DNC trying to undermine my campaign. It goes without saying: the function of the DNC is to represent all of the candidates—to be fair and even-minded. But again, we discussed this many, many months ago, on this show, so what is revealed now is not a shock to me." After the final primary election, Clinton became the presumptive Democratic nominee. On July 12, 2016, Sanders formally endorsed Clinton. He said he would continue working with the Democratic National Convention organizers to implement progressive positions and refused to formally concede before the convention. He spoke at the 2016 Democratic National Convention on July 25, during which he gave full support to Clinton. Some of his supporters attempted to protest Clinton's nomination and booed when Sanders called for party unity. He responded, "Our job is to do two things: to defeat Donald Trump and to elect Hillary Clinton... It is easy to boo, but it is harder to look your kids in the face if we are living under a Trump presidency." On November 8, in the general election, Sanders received nearly 6% of the vote in Vermont, the highest share of a statewide presidential vote for a write-in draft campaign in American history. He also received more votes in Vermont than Gary Johnson, the Libertarian candidate, and Jill Stein, the Green candidate, combined. It was possible to vote for Sanders as a write-in candidate in 12 states, and exact totals were published in California, New Hampshire, and Vermont. In those three states, he received 111,850 write-in votes, about 15% of the nationwide write-in votes, and less than 1% of the total nationwide vote. In November 2016, Sanders's book Our Revolution: A Future to Believe In was released and reached number three on The New York Times Best Seller list. The audiobook later received a Grammy nomination for Best Spoken Word Album. In February 2017, he began webcasting The Bernie Sanders Show on Facebook live streaming. As of April 2, 2017, guests included William Barber, Josh Fox, Jane Mayer, and Bill Nye. Polls taken in 2017 found him to be the most popular politician in the United States. In February 2018, Special Counsel Robert Mueller's investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. elections concluded that Russians had communicated false information during the primary campaigns to help Sanders and Stein and harm Clinton. Sanders rejected the conclusion, stating he had seen no evidence that Russians had helped his campaign. He also questioned the Clinton campaign's lack of action to prevent Russian interference. He later said his campaign had taken action to prevent Russian meddling and that a campaign staffer had alerted the Clinton campaign. Politico noted that a Sanders campaign volunteer contacted a political action committee (PAC) that supported the Clinton campaign to report suspicious activities, but the Sanders campaign did not contact the Clinton campaign as such.

In February 2017, Bernie Sanders began webcasting The Bernie Sanders Show on Facebook live streaming, with guests including William Barber, Josh Fox, Jane Mayer, and Bill Nye as of April 2, 2017. Polls from 2017 found him to be the most popular politician in the United States. In February 2018, Special Counsel Robert Mueller's investigation concluded that Russians had communicated false information during the 2016 primary campaigns to help Sanders and Jill Stein and harm Hillary Clinton; Sanders rejected this conclusion, stating he saw no evidence that Russians had supported his campaign and questioned the Clinton campaign's failure to act against Russian interference. He later claimed his campaign had taken steps to prevent Russian meddling, noting a staffer had alerted the Clinton campaign, though Politico reported that a Sanders volunteer contacted a Clinton-supporting PAC but the campaign did not directly contact the Clinton campaign. In November 2018, the Sanders Institute and Yanis Varoufakis co-founded Progressive International, an international organization to unite progressive activists and organizations in mobilizing people worldwide to transform global institutions. Analysts suggest Sanders's campaign shifted both the Clinton campaign and the Democratic Party politically leftward. In April 2016, Brand New Congress was formed by former campaign staffers to elect congressional representatives with progressive platforms. In August 2016, Sanders founded Our Revolution to educate voters, engage in the political process, and elect progressive candidates at all levels. Susan Page of PBS Newshour described the Democratic Party as "Bernie Sanders's party" in 2018, noting his progressive stance had taken hold, and an April 2018 The Week article suggested "Quietly but steadily, the Democratic Party is admitting that Sanders was right," citing his national single-payer health-care program, $15 minimum wage, free college tuition, and other platform issues. A July 2016 Slate article called the Democratic platform draft "a monument to his campaign," highlighting his support for a $15 minimum wage, Social Security expansion, a carbon tax, Wall Street reform, opposition to the death penalty, and a "reasoned pathway for future legalization" of marijuana. Sanders's presidential campaigns sparked a resurgence of interest in social democracy and democratic socialism among millennials. On February 19, 2019, Sanders announced he would seek the Democratic Party's 2020 presidential nomination; he had declined the Vermont Democratic Party nomination in 2006, 2012, and 2018, leading to an unsuccessful legal challenge in 2016. Along with the announcement, he stated he would abide by a new Democratic Party rule and affirm his party membership. On March 5, 2019, he signed a "loyalty pledge" affirming his Democratic Party membership and commitment to serve as a Democrat if elected. The day before, he had signed paperwork to run as an independent for reelection to his Senate seat in 2024. Sanders's campaign manager was Faiz Shakir, with national co-chairs including Ben Cohen (co-founder of Ben & Jerry's), Representative Ro Khanna, Our Revolution president Nina Turner, and San Juan mayor Carmen Yulín Cruz. Given his high national profile since 2016, NPR described him as "no longer an underdog" when announcing his 2020 campaign. Using the email list built during the 2016 campaign, the 2020 campaign recruited over one million volunteers within weeks, enlisted former NowThis News employees to produce professional videos for social media, live-streamed forums to millions of followers, and launched a podcast and smartphone app for grassroots organizing. The 2020 campaign used similar methods to 2016, avoiding a Super PAC and relying on small-dollar contributions. According to FEC filings, the Sanders campaign raised the most money in the 2020 Democratic field as of June 2019, including funds from his 2018 Senate and 2016 presidential races. In September 2019, the campaign became the fastest in U.S. history to reach one million donors. On October 1, 2019, it announced raising $25.3 million in the third quarter with an average donation of $18, the largest quarterly sum by any Democratic candidate. The campaign raised $34.5 million in the fourth quarter of 2019. Between May and September 2019, Sanders steadily polled between 15% and 20% on most national surveys, according to RealClearPolitics, placing him in second place behind Joe Biden until Elizabeth Warren and Kamala Harris caught up in July. From mid-February 2020 to early March, Sanders polled first in the Democratic primary ahead of Joe Biden and was described as the party's front-runner. A RealClearPolitics analysis found Sanders received the third-most mentions on CNN, Fox News, and MSNBC between January and August 2019, trailing only Biden and Harris, with Biden receiving twice as many mentions. On ABC World News Tonight, Sanders ranked second, trailing Biden by a large margin, though online mentions showed a more balanced picture with Sanders and Warren running neck-and-neck with Biden. On April 6, 2019, Sanders participated in a Fox News town hall that attracted over 2.55 million viewers; his appearance was controversial due to the DNC's decision not to allow Fox to host debates, but it increased Fox viewership by 24% overall and 40% in the 25-to-54 age group, surpassing all other Democratic candidate town halls that year, and had over 1.5 million YouTube views by September 2019. On August 6, 2019, Sanders appeared on The Joe Rogan Experience podcast; some praised Rogan for hosting a pragmatic discussion, while others were stunned by the appearance. After the interview, Rogan stated he is "100% left-wing" and said Sanders "made a ton of sense" and would vote for him; the podcast had over ten million YouTube views by October 2019. In December 2018, the DNC announced a preliminary schedule for 12 official debates beginning in June 2019, with six in 2019 and six in the first four months of 2020. During the July and September debates, commentators described Sanders and Elizabeth Warren as having a "non-aggression pact" due to similar progressive positions compared to more conservative candidates. In the October 15 debate, his first since a heart attack, debate coach Todd Graham gave Sanders an A, his highest rating. In January 2020, CNN hosted the first 2020 debate with six candidates remaining; co-moderator Abby Phillip questioned Sanders and Warren about an allegation that Sanders told Warren in 2018 that a woman could not win the election. Phillip asked Sanders why he said that, ignoring his strong denial, and then asked Warren what she thought when Sanders made that statement. After the debate, Sanders called it ludicrous to believe he doubted a woman's ability to win, noting that Hillary Clinton had beaten Donald Trump by 3 million votes in 2016. On April 8, 2020, Sanders announced he was suspending his campaign, stating he would remain on the ballot in remaining states and continue to accumulate delegates to influence the Democratic Party platform. On April 14, he endorsed Joe Biden, who responded that the endorsement meant a great deal to him and that they were close on many issues, saying he would need Sanders not just to win the campaign but to govern. A self-described democratic socialist, Sanders is a progressive and left-wing populist who admires social democratic programs in Europe and supports workplace democracy through union democracy, worker cooperatives, and workers' management of public enterprises. He is a strong critic of contemporary neoliberal capitalism, which he calls "uber-capitalism," blaming it for declining life expectancy and rising diseases of despair. He advocates universal, single-payer healthcare, paid parental leave, and tuition-free tertiary education. He supports lowering drug costs by reforming patent laws to allow cheaper generic versions in the U.S. and supported the Affordable Care Act, though said it did not go far enough. In November 2015, he gave a speech at Georgetown University on democratic socialism, including its role in the policies of FDR and LBJ. Defining democratic socialism, Sanders said he does not believe government should own the means of production or take over grocery stores, but believes middle-class and working families deserve a decent standard of living and that their incomes should rise, not fall. He supports private companies that create jobs in the U.S. rather than those that profit by exploiting low-wage labor abroad. Based on his positions and votes, many commentators consider his platform primarily focused on tax-funded social benefits inspired by the Nordic model, not social ownership of the means of production. Some socialists and major socialist organizations describe Sanders as a democratic socialist, market socialist, or reformist socialist, while others call him a reformist social democrat. Bhaskar Sunkara characterized Sanders's politics as "class struggle social democracy," arguing that while postwar social democracy operated as a compromise between business, labor, and government, Sanders sees social democratic demands as a means to sharpen class confrontation and raise class consciousness. George Eaton echoed this, saying Sunkara's phrase captures the nuances of Sanders's politics better than a socialist/social democrat binary and that if Sanders were elected, it would represent a new fusion of both. Sanders views global warming as a serious problem and advocates bold action, including substantial investment in infrastructure with goals of energy efficiency, sustainability, and job creation. He considers climate change the greatest threat to national security and said family planning can help fight climate change. He opposed the Dakota Access Pipeline, calling it a climate threat like the Keystone XL Pipeline. In 2019, he announced support for Green New Deal legislation and joined Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Earl Blumenauer in proposing legislation to declare climate change a national and international emergency. Sanders focuses on economic issues such as income and wealth inequality, poverty, raising the minimum wage, universal healthcare, canceling all student debt, making public colleges and universities tuition-free by taxing financial transactions, establishing a 32-hour work week, and expanding Social Security by eliminating the payroll tax cap on incomes over $250,000. He supports laws requiring companies to provide parental leave, sick leave, and vacation time, noting nearly all developed countries have such laws, and supports legislation to make it easier for workers to join or form unions. He opposed the Troubled Asset Relief Program and has called for comprehensive financial reforms, including breaking up "too big to fail" institutions, restoring Glass–Steagall legislation, reforming the Federal Reserve, and allowing the Post Office to offer basic financial services in marginalized communities. He voted against and has long opposed NAFTA, CAFTA, and PNTR with China, calling them a "disaster for the American worker" due to job losses abroad, and opposes the Trans-Pacific Partnership, which he says was "written by corporate America and the pharmaceutical industry and Wall Street." On May 1, 2019, he tweeted that since voting against the China trade deal, America had lost over three million manufacturing jobs. He strongly opposes outsourcing American jobs. During discussions of the United States Innovation and Competition Act, he proposed a measure to ensure funded semiconductor companies could not outsource jobs or forbid employee unionization; the proposal was voted down by most Democrats and all Republicans in the Senate. Ahead of the 2022 midterms, Sanders said the Democratic Party should focus more on supporting unionization, proposing that if 50% of workers in a bargaining unit plus one vote to form a union, they have a union. He supports establishing worker-owned cooperatives and introduced legislation from the 1990s to the 2020s to aid workers in forming their own businesses or worker-owned cooperatives. As early as 1976, Sanders proposed workplace democracy, saying major industries should be publicly owned and controlled by workers. He supports empowering and expanding labor unions to advance union democracy. In 1987, he defined democracy as public ownership and workers' self-management, stating that democracy means public ownership of major means of production, decentralization, and involving people in their work, replacing bosses and workers with democratic control over factories and shops. In his 2020 presidential run, he proposed that 20% of stocks in corporations with over $100 million in annual revenue be owned by workers and that 45% of the board of directors of such corporations be elected by workers. Sanders supports reducing military spending while pursuing more diplomacy and international cooperation. He opposed funding the Nicaraguan contras in the CIA's covert war against Nicaragua's leftist government, opposed the U.S. invasion of Iraq, and criticized policies during the war on terror, particularly mass surveillance and the USA Patriot Act. He criticized Israel's actions during the 2014 Gaza war and U.S. involvement in the Saudi-led intervention in Yemen.

Bernie Sanders defines democracy as public ownership of the major means of production, decentralization, and people's involvement in their work, emphasizing democratic control over factories and shops to the greatest extent possible. In his 2020 presidential campaign, he proposed that workers own 20% of the stocks in corporations with over $100 million in annual revenue and that 45% of the board of directors of such corporations be elected by workers. Sanders supports reducing military spending and promotes diplomacy and international cooperation, opposing funding for the Nicaraguan contras and the U.S. invasion of Iraq, as well as policies like mass surveillance and the USA Patriot Act. He criticized Israel’s actions during the 2014 Gaza war and U.S. involvement in the Saudi-led intervention in Yemen. In response to the Islamic State’s attacks in Paris in November 2015, he warned against Islamophobia and urged the U.S. to welcome Syrian refugees, and he condemned the 2020 assassination of Iranian general Qasem Soleimani as a dangerous escalation. Sanders supports Palestinian rights and consistently upholds Israel’s right to exist, calling the American Israel Public Affairs Committee a platform for bigotry and opposing Trump’s recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital, which he said would harm peace efforts. During the Gaza war, he criticized both Hamas for the October 7 attacks and Israel for its bombing of Gaza, initially calling for a pause in fighting and later advocating for a humanitarian ceasefire and urging Biden to withhold military aid to Israel. He accused Israel of mass starvation, ethnic cleansing, and extermination, and in September 2025 stated that the intent to commit genocide in Gaza is clear and inescapable. In a 2017 speech at Westminster College, Sanders advocated for greater international collaboration, adherence to agreements like the Paris Agreement and Iran nuclear deal, and promoted human rights and democratic ideals, warning against global economic inequality and climate change, and asserting that U.S. military use must be a last resort. He criticized U.S. support for "murderous regimes" during the Cold War, such as in Iran, Chile, and El Salvador, and condemned Russian interference in the 2016 election and Trump’s handling of it. He does not view Turkey as a U.S. ally and opposed the Turkish military offensive against U.S.-aligned Kurdish forces in northeastern Syria. Sanders supports closing the gun show loophole, banning assault weapons, and implementing universal federal background checks. In 1990, his campaign benefited from the NRA opposing Peter Smith, who had reversed his stance on firearm restrictions. In 1993, as a U.S. representative, he voted against the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act and in 2005 supported legislation granting gun manufacturers legal immunity, though by 2016 he said he would support repealing it. In 1996, he opposed CDC funding for firearm research, but in 2016 called for increased CDC funding for gun violence studies. Sanders has long held progressive views, identifying as a feminist, supporting abortion rights, opposing defunding Planned Parenthood, advocating for LGBT rights (including supporting same-sex marriage in Vermont in 2009), denouncing institutional racism, calling for criminal justice reform, supporting a crackdown on police brutality, abolishing private for-profit prisons and the death penalty, supporting Black Lives Matter, and advocating for federal legalization of marijuana. He supports campaign finance reform and a constitutional amendment or judicial decision to overturn Citizens United v. FEC. Sanders criticized Trump for appointing multiple billionaires to his cabinet, rolled back the Clean Power Plan, and warned against the Syrian Civil War, stating it is easier to enter than exit. In 2017, he pledged to defeat "Trump and Trumpism and the Republican right-wing ideology." He responded to Trump’s 2018 State of the Union by calling him "compulsively dishonest" and criticizing his termination of DACA, as well as his failure to acknowledge Russian interference in the 2016 election. On January 6, 2021, after the Capitol attack, Sanders stated that Trump would go down in history as the worst and most dangerous president. He voted to convict Trump on both articles of his first impeachment in 2020 and on the sole article of his second in 2021. Sanders influenced the Biden administration’s environmental policy, with Biden’s team adopting climate recommendations from the Biden–Sanders Unity Task Force. After Biden’s election, speculation arose about Sanders being appointed Labor Secretary, supported by progressive groups like the Sunrise Movement, though he said he would accept the nomination if offered, and Boston mayor Marty Walsh was chosen instead. Biden confirmed discussing the position with Sanders, but both agreed that Sanders’s resignation and special election would risk the Democrats’ slim Senate majority. On February 23, 2021, Sanders became the first Democratic senator to oppose a Biden cabinet pick, voting against Tom Vilsack’s confirmation as Agriculture Secretary due to concerns about his past lobbying and corporate ties. In 2022, he signed letters to Vilsack and Solicitor General Elizabeth Prelogar supporting California’s Proposition 12 on farm animal welfare. Sanders supported Senate Democrats using budget reconciliation to pass the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021, which passed 50–49 and was signed by Biden on March 11, 2021. He has remained a key influence in the Biden administration, noting it was a strange experience to have such influence after writing a book called *Outsider in the House*, and stated their relationship, lasting over 30 years, is based on mutual respect and trust. Before the 2022 midterms, Sanders called it the most consequential midterm election in modern U.S. history, fearing the Democratic Party had not effectively reached young and working-class voters. Sanders was the only independent or Democratic senator to oppose the CHIPS and Science Act, joining 17 Republican senators, calling it "crony capitalism," and setting conditions including equity issuance to the federal government, no stock buybacks, no outsourcing American jobs, maintaining collective bargaining agreements, and neutrality in union organizing. In April 2023, Sanders endorsed Biden in the 2024 presidential election, and after Biden withdrew, endorsed Harris at the Democratic National Convention. To appeal to pro-Palestinian critics, he said that after Harris wins, they would change U.S. policy toward Netanyahu and emphasized Trump’s policies on climate change, minimum wage, and tax cuts for the wealthy. Trump’s 2024 reelection sparked concern among Democrats, with the three richest men attending his inauguration and policies like Project 2025—reducing corporate and capital gains taxes, instituting a flat income tax, cutting Medicare and Medicaid, reversing Biden’s policies, and weakening environmental protections—being seen as myopic and unconstitutional. After Trump won, Sanders blamed the Democratic Party’s abandonment of working-class people for its defeat. In February 2025, Sanders launched the "Fighting Oligarchy Tour" with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to criticize Trump’s policies and economic inequality. In April 2025, he criticized the administration for moving "rapidly toward oligarchy" and called the U.S. a "pseudo-democracy." At a June 2025 rally, Sanders reacted to Trump’s bombing of Iranian nuclear sites by saying the American people were being lied to again and history should not repeat. In June 2025, he endorsed Zohran Mamdani for the 2025 New York City Democratic mayoral primary, calling him the "best choice," and in September 2025 criticized Democratic officials for not supporting Mamdani after his primary victory. In the same month, Sanders interviewed Mamdani about his political beginnings and achievements as mayor and senator. On September 15, 2025, Sanders stated that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, becoming the first U.S. senator to make such a comment. Born into a Democratic-voting family, Sanders first engaged in political activism when his brother Larry campaigned for Adlai Stevenson II in 1956. He joined the Liberty Union Party in 1971, served as party chairman, and left in 1977 to become an independent. In 1980, he served as an elector for the Socialist Workers Party. In 1981, he ran as an independent for mayor of Burlington, Vermont, defeating the Democratic incumbent and was reelected three times. Though an independent, he endorsed Walter Mondale in 1984 (with a lukewarm statement) and Jesse Jackson in 1988 enthusiastically, with the Jackson campaign inspiring closer ties to the Democratic Party. He spoke at the 1983 Socialist Party USA conference. Sanders first ran for the U.S. House in 1988 and for the U.S. Senate in 2006, often winning the Democratic primary to eliminate challengers and then running as an independent in the general election. He continued this strategy in his 2018 Senate reelection. Throughout his congressional tenure, he has been listed as an independent, caucusing with Democrats in the House and continuing to caucus with Democrats in the Senate. Some conservative southern Democrats initially barred him from the caucus due to concerns about his socialist views, but he soon worked constructively with Democrats, voting with the party over 90% of the time. Starting with his 2016 campaign, Sanders signaled he was running as a Democrat and would run as one in future elections. When challenged by Clinton, he said, "Of course I am a Democrat and running for the Democratic nomination." His Senate website and press materials continued to refer to him as an independent during the campaign and after returning to the Senate. In October 2017, he said he would run as an independent in 2018 despite pressure to run as a Democrat. In March 2019, he signed a formal "loyalty pledge" to the Democratic Party, stating he was a member and would serve as a Democrat if elected president, the day after signing paperwork to run as an independent for Senate reelection in 2024. After Trump’s 2016 victory, Sanders urged the Democratic Party to reform, break free from corporate ties, and become a grassroots party of working people, the elderly, and the poor, drawing parallels to the UK Labour Party’s 2017 election. He wrote in The New York Times that the British elections should be a lesson for the Democrats, urging them to abandon a cautious, centrist ideology and embrace a progressive manifesto that energized young people and workers, and had earlier praised Jeremy Corbyn’s stance on class issues. Sanders is one of two independents in the Senate, alongside Angus King, both of whom caucus with Democrats. In 1963, Sanders and Deborah Shiling Messing volunteered on the Israeli kibbutz Sha'ar HaAmakim, married in 1964, bought a summer home in Vermont, had no children, and divorced in 1966. His only biological child, Levi Sanders, was born in 1969 to then-girlfriend Susan Campbell Mott. On May 28, 1988, Sanders married Jane O'Meara Driscoll, who later became president of Burlington College. The day after their wedding, they visited the Soviet Union as part of an official delegation. They own a row house in Capitol Hill, a house in Burlington’s New North End, and a lakefront summer home in North Hero. He considers Jane’s three children—Dave (born 1975), Carina (born 1974), and Heather Titus (born 1971)—to be his own. Sanders’s elder brother, Larry, lives in England.

Bernie Sanders was divorced in 1966 and had one biological child, Levi Sanders, born in 1969 to his then-girlfriend Susan Campbell Mott. On May 28, 1988, he married Jane O'Meara Driscoll (née Mary Jane O'Meara), who later became president of Burlington College in Burlington, Vermont. The day after their wedding, the couple visited the Soviet Union as part of an official delegation in Sanders’s capacity as mayor. They own a row house in Capitol Hill, a house in Burlington’s New North End neighborhood, and a lakefront summer home in North Hero. Sanders considers Jane’s three children—Dave Driscoll (born 1975), Carina Driscoll (born 1974), and Heather Titus (née Driscoll; born 1971)—to be his own. His elder brother, Larry, lives in England and was a Green Party county councillor representing the East Oxford division on Oxfordshire County Council until he retired in 2013; he ran as a Green Party candidate for Oxford West and Abingdon in the 2015 British general election and came in fifth. Sanders told CNN, "I owe my brother an enormous amount. It was my brother who actually introduced me to a lot of my ideas." On October 1, 2019, Sanders was hospitalized after experiencing chest pains at a campaign event in Las Vegas; his campaign announced the next day that a blockage had been found in one coronary artery and two stents were inserted. Scheduled events were canceled until further notice, and two days later, his campaign released a statement that he had been diagnosed with a heart attack; he was released from the hospital the same day. The statement from his doctors stated that after presenting to an outside facility with chest pain, Sen. Sanders was diagnosed with a myocardial infarction, was transferred to Desert Springs Hospital Medical Center, and had two stents placed in a blocked coronary artery in a timely fashion, with all other arteries being normal. His hospital course was uneventful, and he was discharged with instructions to follow up with his personal physician. A few days after returning home, Sanders addressed media and said he had experienced fatigue and chest discomfort for a month or two before the incident, expressing regret for not seeking medical assessment sooner: "I was dumb." He made his first national appearance after the heart attack on October 15 at a Democratic debate, saying, "I'm healthy, I'm feeling great," and stated that mounting a vigorous campaign would reassure voters about his health and ability to serve as president. He was noted to be "lively and sharp" at the debate. In December 2019, three months after the heart attack, Sanders released letters from three physicians—Attending Physician of Congress Brian P. Monahan and two cardiologists—declaring him healthy and recovered. On December 4, 2015, Sanders won Time's 2015 Person of the Year readers' poll with 10.2% of the vote but did not receive the editorial board's award. On March 20, 2016, he was given an honorary Lushootseed name, dxʷshudičup, by Deborah Parker in Seattle to honor his focus on Native American issues. On May 30, 2017, he received an honorary degree of Doctor of Humane Letters from Brooklyn College. In a 2016 speech describing his upbringing as an American Jew, Sanders noted that his father generally attended synagogue only on Yom Kippur, his mother chafed at his yeshiva Sunday schooling, and their religious observances were mostly limited to Passover seders with neighbors; Larry Sanders said their parents were pleased to be Jews but did not have a strong belief in God. Bernie had a bar mitzvah at the historic Kingsway Jewish Center in Midwood, Brooklyn. In 1963, Sanders and his first wife volunteered at Sha'ar HaAmakim, a kibbutz in northern Israel, through the Labor Zionist youth movement Hashomer Hatzair, motivated by both socialistic and Zionist ideals. As mayor of Burlington, Sanders allowed a Chabad public menorah to be placed at city hall, an action contested by the ACLU; he publicly inaugurated the Hanukkah menorah and performed the blessing of Hanukkah candles, an action that played a significant role in the global spread of public menorah celebrations. Sanders has said he is "proud to be Jewish" and describes himself as "not particularly religious" and "not actively involved" with organized religion, though a press package lists his religion as Jewish. He believes in God but not necessarily in a traditional way, stating, "I think everyone believes in God in their own ways," and that "all of us are connected, all of life is connected, and that we are all tied together." On October 2015, during a Jimmy Kimmel Live! appearance, when asked about his Jewish heritage and belief in God, Sanders replied, "I am who I am, and what I believe in and what my spirituality is about is that we're all in this together. That I think it is not a good thing to believe as human beings we can turn our backs on the suffering of other people... and this is not Judaism, this is what Pope Francis is talking about, that we can't just worship billionaires and the making of more and more money. Life is more than that." In 2016, he disclosed having "very strong religious and spiritual feelings," adding, "My spirituality is that we are all in this together and that when children go hungry, when veterans sleep out on the street, it impacts me." Sanders does not regularly attend synagogue and does not refrain from working on Rosh Hashanah; he has attended yahrzeit observances and in 2015 participated in a Tashlikh ceremony with the mayor of Lynchburg on Rosh Hashanah. According to Richard Sugarman, his Jewish identity is "certainly more ethnic and cultural than religious." His wife is Roman Catholic, and he has expressed admiration for Pope Francis, saying the Catholic Church leader is raising profound issues and that he feels very close to Francis’s economic teachings, describing him as "incredibly smart and brave." In April 2016, he accepted an invitation from Marcelo Sánchez Sorondo, an aide close to Francis, to speak at a Vatican conference on economic and environmental issues and met briefly with Francis. In December 1987, during his tenure as mayor, Sanders recorded a folk album, We Shall Overcome, with 30 Vermont musicians, performing his vocals in a talking blues style. Due to his two high-profile campaigns in 2016 and 2020, Sanders and his campaigns have generated many Internet memes and online content. The Facebook group Bernie Sanders' Dank Meme Stash, where users submit memes centered on Sanders, gained significant attention during the 2016 primary season. During the 2020 primary season, a still from a fundraising video in which Sanders says, "I am once again asking for your financial support," went viral, with numerous edits made. The day before Super Tuesday 2020, a video of Twitch streamer Neekolul wearing a Bernie 2020 shirt and lip-syncing "Oki Doki Boomer" went viral. In 2021, a frame from Joe Biden’s inauguration showing Sanders in a folding chair wearing patterned mittens and a jacket similar to the one in the "I am once again asking" meme went viral, with the image edited into other scenes. Sanders appeared in a cameo in the 1988 film Sweet Hearts Dance, playing a man who distributes candy to trick-or-treaters. In 1999, he acted in My X-Girlfriend's Wedding Reception as Rabbi Manny Shevitz, mourning the Brooklyn Dodgers’ move to Los Angeles, reflecting his Brooklyn upbringing. On February 6, 2016, he was a guest star alongside Larry David (a sixth cousin once removed of Sanders) on Saturday Night Live, playing a Polish immigrant on a steamship sinking near the Statue of Liberty. In the DC Extended Universe film Birds of Prey (and the Fantabulous Emancipation of One Harley Quinn), Roman Sionis wants Harley Quinn dead because she "voted for Bernie."
